text.paragraph: New patient visit for four months of wheeze, night cough and breathlessness on exertion in a 72-year-old woman with long-standing asthma that was never confirmed: examination, chest X-ray, ECG, blood tests and BNP, and planning of lung function testing and an echocardiogram [S]
This fictional modern episode addresses the presenting concerns below. [S]

list.item: Her breathing wakes her at night and stops her climbing stairs, and she has had to travel less. [S]
She has been told for years that it is asthma, or her weight, or her heart, and wants to know for certain which it is. [S]
She wants to keep going to Washington for the council's meetings. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Mary Jane McLeod was born on July 10, 1875, near Mayesville, South Carolina, the fifteenth of seventeen children of Samuel and Patsy McLeod. Her parents, and eight of her older siblings, had been enslaved; after emancipation the family bought five acres of land and farmed cotton. [D]

She was the only McLeod child to get an education, first at a Presbyterian mission school near Mayesville and then at Scotia Seminary. In 1898 she married Albertus Bethune; they separated after about nine years without divorcing, and he died in 1918. [D]

In 1904 she founded a school for Black girls in Daytona Beach, Florida. She opened McLeod Hospital there in 1911, which the National Park Service says played a critical role in containing the influenza pandemic of 1918, and she and her students faced down the Ku Klux Klan at the school. The school merged with the Cookman Institute (dated 1923 by the National Park Service; named Bethune-Cookman College in 1929 according to another reference), and she was its president until 1942. [D]

She was president of the National Association of Colored Women from 1924, received the NAACP's Spingarn Medal in 1935, and founded the National Council of Negro Women on December 5, 1935. She directed the Division of Negro Affairs of the National Youth Administration from the mid-1930s until it closed in 1943 and led the informal group of Black federal advisers known as the Black Cabinet. She said of her place in Washington: "When they see me, they know that the Negro is present." [D]

For many years she suffered from chronic asthma, which increasingly restricted her ability to travel, and after a particularly severe attack in 1942 she gave up the presidency of Bethune-Cookman College. [D]

The guide to her foundation's papers lists "Bethune asthma attacks" as a major topic of her administrative correspondence in the first half of 1943, and describes her health problems as a recurrent subject of her correspondence in those years. [D]

From 1935 she lived in a series of apartments in Washington, D.C., while keeping her home, known as the Retreat, on the campus in Daytona Beach. In December 1943 she and the National Council of Negro Women bought 1318 Vermont Avenue, which became the council's first national headquarters and her Washington residence. [D]

list.item: Retired college president who still chairs a national women's organization and travels to Washington, D.C., for its board meetings every month or two; lives in her own house on the campus in Daytona Beach and stays in the organization's Washington headquarters when she is there [S]

Lives alone; separated from her husband long before his death decades ago; a son and grandchildren live nearby; colleagues and church members visit daily. No relative is named or given a role in her care [S]

Grew up in a large farming family in South Carolina whose parents had been enslaved; has spent her life working against segregation, and has met clinicians who dismissed her breathlessness as her weight or her age [S]
Never smoked; no vaping; no wood stove at home; no alcohol; no occupational dust or chemical exposure [S]
Triggers she has noticed: colds, dust when papers and books are moved, strong perfume at meetings, and humid summer air; no pets; the house has central air conditioning [S]

tr.td: Albuterol 90 mcg/actuation inhaler, two puffs as needed, from an urgent care visit four months ago (used alone, without an inhaled steroid)
Two puffs every 4 hours as needed; she uses it most days

tr.td: Wheeze, cough and breathlessness for four months: waking with cough and tight chest two or three nights a week, breathless on one flight of stairs, relieved by albuterol, worse with colds, dust and strong scents; known asthma for many years but never confirmed by lung function testing and never treated with an inhaled steroid. Asthma, COPD and heart failure to be distinguished: spirometry with bronchodilator response, FeNO and an echocardiogram booked
S — Synthetic presenting problem anchored to her documented chronic asthma. Superseded by the diagnosis at the second visit.
Blocked nose, thick postnasal drip and a reduced sense of smell for years, worse in the last year; no nosebleeds; never seen by an ear, nose and throat specialist
S — Synthetic upper-airway symptoms; superseded by the diagnosis of chronic rhinosinusitis after nasal endoscopy.
Gastro-esophageal reflux: heartburn and an acid taste two or three evenings a week, worse after late meals and lying down; no trouble swallowing, vomiting, black stools or weight loss
S — Synthetic comorbidity of asthma; not a claim about her real health.
Obesity, class 1 (BMI 33.1); she wants to walk more and to keep up with her work, and agreed to talk about it
S — Synthetic comorbidity recorded in her words and with her agreement; not a claim about her real weight.

Asthma, COPD and heart failure to be distinguished: spirometry with bronchodilator response, FeNO and an echocardiogram booked: active, confirmed [S]
Blocked nose, thick postnasal drip and a reduced sense of smell for years, worse in the last year; no nosebleeds; never seen by an ear, nose and throat specialist: active, confirmed [S]

Pulmonology consultation in two weeks with spirometry before and after bronchodilator, DLCO and FeNO, to confirm or refute asthma, separate it from COPD and heart disease, and plan treatment. Guideline: CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, asthma and hypertension monographs (2026); Global Strategy for Asthma Management and Prevention, 2025 update (2025); 2020 Focused Updates to the Asthma Management Guidelines: A Report from the National Asthma Education and Prevention Program Coordinating Committee Expert Panel Working Group (2020) [S]

Work-up of wheeze and breathlessness: chest X-ray, ECG, blood count with eosinophils, BNP, TSH and kidney function today; transthoracic echocardiogram before the consultation; albuterol continued as needed until testing, holding it for six hours before spirometry. Guideline: Global Strategy for Asthma Management and Prevention, 2025 update (2025); 2020 Focused Updates to the Asthma Management Guidelines: A Report from the National Asthma Education and Prevention Program Coordinating Committee Expert Panel Working Group (2020); Heidenreich PA, et al. 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure: Executive Summary. J Am Coll Cardiol 2022;79(17):1757-1780 (PMID 35379504) (2022) [S]

Home blood pressure readings twice daily for a week, with a validated upper-arm cuff, because clinic readings are raised. Guideline: CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, asthma and hypertension monographs (2026); 2025 AHA/ACC/AANP/AAPA/ABC/ACCP/ACPM/AGS/AMA/ASPC/NMA/PCNA/SGIM Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation, and Management of High Blood Pressure in Adults (2025) [S]

Equity safeguards: spirometry read with race-neutral GLI Global equations, plain explanation of every result, and a check at each visit that her symptoms are not put down to her weight or age. Guideline: Bhakta NR, et al. Race and Ethnicity in Pulmonary Function Test Interpretation: An Official American Thoracic Society Statement. Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2023;207(8):978-995 (PMID 36973004) (2023); Pate CA, et al. Asthma Surveillance - United States, 2006-2018. MMWR Surveill Summ 2021;70(5):1-32 (PMID 34529643) (2021) [S]
